description: I really like space…It is mostly empty, and every mission that answers one question just asks back several more. Maybe it is our human nature to ask the unknown. Even the silly questions. Are we alone? Are we not?
summary:
Meet Lucy. She has a dream: to design a mission to space. The only problem is that she's leaving every decision to you.

Lucy's Dream is an interactive game I built to turn space mission design into something you can play. You choose the objective, architecture, spacecraft, payload, trajectory, communications, launch and operations, and every choice pushes back. Mass, power, cost, risk, data and scientific return are all pulling against each other, and you have to find a balance.

Pick an ambitious payload and your science might soar, but can your spacecraft actually carry and power it? Play it safe and you might strip out the very thing that made the mission exciting.

Lucy guides you through each stage, then judges the mission you've built and shows you where things could have gone differently.

I made Lucy's Dream because systems engineering is usually taught through diagrams and textbooks, and I wanted to put it in the player's hands instead. Here, the trade-offs become part of the adventure, and experimenting, failing and trying again are all part of the mission.
details:
A big part of building Lucy's Dream was asking myself how to make mission design feel like a game rather than homework.

I built it as a web app using React, TypeScript, HTML and CSS, with GitHub for managing the project and Vercel for deployment. The game runs across multiple phases, with interactive choices, animated dialogue and a scoring system that remembers what the player has done, so each screen isn't just a separate quiz.

I used NASA-provided resources to ground the engineering content, but I deliberately translated it into something a player can follow without already knowing spacecraft engineering. The hard part was deciding what complexity to keep and what to cut. Too little, and the decisions stop meaning anything. Too much, and suddenly the player needs a calculator and an aerospace degree.

That balance shaped everything from how much information appears on screen to the pacing of Lucy's dialogue. I also put a lot of time into the visual identity. The futuristic interface, spacecraft imagery, animations and Lucy herself are all there to make players feel like they're progressing through their own mission, not clicking through an educational webpage.

Throughout development I kept coming back to accuracy, accessibility, visual design, pacing, replayability and player freedom. Ultimately, I wanted learning to happen naturally while the player is busy trying to build something that could actually make it to space.
